question: Explain the LIFO principle of a stack and describe what happens during push and pop operations.
expected_points: LIFO stands for Last In, First Out: the last element added is the first one removed
Push adds an element to the top of the stack
Pop removes and returns the top element of the stack
critical_misconceptions: Stack operates on First In, First Out (FIFO)
Pop removes the oldest or bottom element
Elements can be added or removed from any arbitrary index in a standard stack
hint: Think of a physical stack of dinner plates or trays where you can only add or remove from the very top.

question: What is the purpose of the peek (or top) operation on a stack, and what error occurs if you try to pop from an empty stack?
expected_points: Peek (or top) examines the value of the top element without removing it from the stack
Attempting to pop or peek from an empty stack causes stack underflow (an underflow error or exception)
Stack overflow occurs when attempting to push onto a fixed-size stack that has reached maximum capacity
critical_misconceptions: Peek modifies the stack by removing the top element
Popping an empty stack returns the last pushed item
hint: Consider whether looking at the top item should change the stack's size, and what happens when nothing is there to remove.

question: Describe two practical applications of stacks in computer systems or software development, and explain why a stack is the ideal data structure for them.
expected_points: Function call stack / recursion management: tracks active function frames and return addresses in LIFO order
Balanced parentheses / syntax validation: pushes opening delimiters and pops to match closing delimiters
Undo/Redo mechanisms or expression evaluation / backtracking (e.g. DFS)
critical_misconceptions: Breadth-first search (BFS) uses a stack by default
The call stack operates as First In, First Out
hint: Think about how your programming language tracks active function calls or how a text editor undoes your most recent keystrokes.

question: What is the time complexity of the core stack operations (push, pop, peek), and how do array-based vs linked-list-based implementations differ?
expected_points: Core operations (push, pop, peek) operate in O(1) constant time
Array-based implementation offers fast cache locality but may require O(n) dynamic resizing when capacity is reached
Linked-list-based implementation guarantees strict O(1) per operation without resizing, but incurs extra memory overhead for pointers
critical_misconceptions: Push or pop in a stack requires O(n) linear time because elements must shift
Array and linked list implementations have identical memory overhead
hint: Remember that all stack operations occur only at one end (the top), meaning no shifting of remaining elements is required.

question: What is a monotonic stack, and how does it achieve an overall O(n) time complexity for problems like finding the 'Next Greater Element' for all array items?
expected_points: A monotonic stack maintains its elements in strictly increasing or decreasing order
When processing a new element, elements that violate the monotonic property are popped
Overall time complexity is O(n) because each element is pushed onto the stack at most once and popped at most once (amortized O(1) per element)
critical_misconceptions: A nested while-loop inside the traversal automatically makes the algorithm O(n^2)
A monotonic stack requires sorting the entire array first
hint: Consider the total life cycle of any single element: how many times can it enter and leave the stack across the whole array scan?

question: Explain the FIFO principle of a queue and describe the primary operations: enqueue and dequeue.
expected_points: FIFO stands for First In, First Out: the first element added is the first one to be removed
Enqueue adds an element to the rear (or tail/back) of the queue
Dequeue removes and returns the element from the front (or head) of the queue
critical_misconceptions: Queue operates on Last In, First Out (LIFO)
Enqueue and dequeue happen at the same end of the data structure
hint: Think of a checkout queue or ticket line: the person who arrives first gets served first.

question: How do the front and rear pointers track elements in a queue, and what happens when you attempt to dequeue from an empty queue?
expected_points: Front pointer indicates the position of the next element to be removed; rear pointer indicates where new elements are inserted
Queue is empty when front equals rear (or front exceeds rear, depending on convention/implementation)
Attempting to dequeue from an empty queue results in queue underflow (an error or exception)
critical_misconceptions: Rear pointer points to the next item to be removed
Dequeuing from an empty queue returns the front element from a previous session
hint: Track the indices: which pointer moves forward when an item arrives, and which moves when an item is served?

question: Why is a circular queue preferred over a linear array queue, and how does modulo arithmetic solve the problem of false overflow?
expected_points: In a linear array queue, dequeuing leaves unused space at the front, causing 'false overflow' even when capacity remains
A circular queue wraps rear and front pointers back to index 0 using modulo arithmetic: (index + 1) % capacity
This reuses freed memory slots efficiently without shifting elements
critical_misconceptions: Linear queues automatically shift all elements on every dequeue without performance cost
Circular queues require a circular doubly linked list
hint: What happens when the rear pointer reaches the end of the array, but several items have already been dequeued from the front?

question: Discuss practical applications of queues in operating systems and algorithms, highlighting why FIFO ordering is essential.
expected_points: Operating system CPU scheduling / print spooling / message buffers (ensures tasks are processed in fair order of arrival)
Breadth-First Search (BFS) in trees and graphs: explores all nodes level-by-level in the order they were discovered
Asynchronous request handling and rate limiting (producer-consumer pattern)
critical_misconceptions: Depth-First Search (DFS) relies on a queue
LIFO order is needed for fair printer job spooling
hint: Consider why level-by-level exploration in a tree requires visiting older discovered nodes before newer ones.

question: Explain how to implement a FIFO queue using two LIFO stacks, and analyze the time complexity of the enqueue and dequeue operations.
expected_points: Use two stacks: an input stack (in_stack) for enqueue and an output stack (out_stack) for dequeue
Enqueue pushes directly onto in_stack in O(1) time
Dequeue pops from out_stack; if out_stack is empty, transfer all elements from in_stack to out_stack (reversing their order) and pop
Each element is transferred at most once, giving an amortized time complexity of O(1) per dequeue
critical_misconceptions: Transferring elements back and forth on every single dequeue or enqueue is required
The worst-case O(n) transfer means the average/amortized performance is also O(n)
hint: Two negatives make a positive: reversing a reversed sequence restores the original FIFO order.
